page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a), the [HYPOTHESIS] paragraph beginning 'for the canonical 2,000-user workload'
quoted_clause: the incremental per-request compute cost of the 768-dim (all-mpnet) vs 384-dim (MiniLM) embedding models — a cross-model difference, not a dim-only sweep — is ~11.1 GFLOP per 64-token query (2 × params × L: 14.08 − 2.94 GFLOP, the §3(a) embedding table's own rows; a same-family 384-dim variant halves index storage (encoder compute ~unchanged)) — ~56–370 ms if encoded on a single CPU core at a realistic 30–200 GFLOP/s, but only ~1.1 ms on a ~10 TFLOP/s GPU, which is the basis the ~120 ms retrieval budget already assumes (vector search and reranking on a local GPU, Ch 4). On that basis the incremental cost stays well within the ~120 ms retrieval budget; single-core encoding fits only at the high end of that throughput range (55.5 ms at 200 GFLOP/s vs 370 ms at 30 GFLOP/s) — conditional on measured single-core throughput. The decision hinges on whether the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain (an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS], domain- and corpus-specific — §5.3) translates into sufficient answer-quality improvement to justify the ~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64-token query, Table 5-1) — a workload-specific tradeoff, not a universal rule.
observed: A single ~200-word paragraph embeds six distinct calculations (FLOP delta, CPU time range, GPU time, budget comparison, single-core throughput range, MAP-vs-FLOP tradeoff) with nested parentheticals and cross-references. The reader must hold all intermediate values in working memory to follow the argument. The paragraph's intellectual job is to show that the 768-dim choice is compute-justified and that the quality claim remains unvalidated, but the density obscures both points.
evidence: All individual numbers are arithmetically correct (14.08−2.94=11.14≈11.1; 11.1/200=55.5 ms; 11.1/30=370 ms; 11.1/10000=1.11 ms; 14.08/2.94≈4.8×). The problem is presentation, not correctness.
root_cause: The paragraph attempts to do the full quantitative comparison and the qualitative recommendation in one block, without separating the computation from the decision logic.
correction: Split into two or three shorter paragraphs: (1) the FLOP delta and its time implications on CPU vs GPU (a short table or 2–3 sentences); (2) the budget comparison (one sentence: 'on the GPU basis the ~1.1 ms incremental cost is negligible against the 120 ms retrieval budget'); (3) the decision logic (the MAP-vs-FLOP tradeoff, with the [HYPOTHESIS] label on the MAP claim). This preserves all content while reducing cognitive load.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the three distinct intellectual moves (compute cost, budget fit, quality tradeoff) without re-reading the paragraph more than once.

page_hint: Ch 5, §1, 'Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict'
quoted_clause: Parallel refinement (diffusion-style decoding that updates many token positions per step) is worth investigating when low-batch latency or constrained infilling dominates, but neither advantage follows from a model-family label. AR fill-in-the-middle (FIM) models — autoregressive models trained to infill a marked span — are a necessary editing baseline.
observed: This section introduces diffusion-style decoding and FIM models as candidate inference modes, but the canonical RAG workload (and the rest of the chapter) uses standard autoregressive generation. The section's connection to the chapter's main argument (workload-driven model selection for the canonical RAG system) is not made explicit. A reader may wonder why these modes are relevant to an enterprise Q&A RAG tool. The section also introduces the term 'infilling' without defining it in the context of the canonical workload.
evidence: The canonical workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2) specifies a 9.2K-input, 300-output AR generation task. No part of the chapter's worked example uses diffusion or FIM. The section's last sentence ('The selection question is whether the specific model, sampler and runtime meet the workload's quality, output and SLO requirements together') is a general principle that applies to AR as well.
root_cause: The section was written to cover the general principle that inference mode is a selection dimension, but the examples chosen (diffusion, FIM) are not the mode used by the canonical workload, creating a disconnect between the principle and the worked example.
correction: Either (a) add one sentence connecting the principle to the canonical workload: 'For the canonical RAG workload, the inference mode is standard autoregressive generation; the selection question reduces to whether the chosen AR model, tokenizer, and serving runtime meet the SLOs. For workloads that might use non-AR generation (editing, infilling, image-to-text), the mode itself becomes an additional selection dimension.' Or (b) move the diffusion/FIM discussion to a brief footnote or a 'beyond the canonical workload' sidebar, keeping the main text focused on the AR case the chapter actually works through.
acceptance_test: A reader can see why the inference-mode discussion is relevant to the canonical RAG workload without inferring the connection themselves.

page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Latency Is a Distribution, Not a Mean' — the p99 explanation
quoted_clause: a knife-edge property of this N = 10,000 sample, not of the distribution: linear interpolation lands on the largest non-straggler draw, while the population p99 of the stated 99% log-normal + 1% straggler mixture is 5.0 s (one extra straggler, 101 of 10,000, moves the sample p99 to 5.0 s too)
observed: The explanation of why the sample p99 is 1.33 s while the population p99 is 5.0 s is technically correct but requires the reader to hold in mind: (a) the sample composition (9,900 log-normal + 100 stragglers), (b) the linear-interpolation method for percentiles, (c) the CDF jump at 5.0 s in the population, and (d) the sensitivity to one extra straggler. The 'knife-edge' framing is apt but the mechanism is not made concrete enough for a first reading. A reader who is not already fluent in order-statistic interpolation may accept the conclusion without understanding why.
evidence: The math is correct: with 10,000 samples, p99 is at rank 9,901 (1-indexed). The 9,900th value is the max log-normal draw (~1.33 s); the 9,901st is a straggler at 5.0 s. Linear interpolation between ranks 9,900 and 9,901 at the 0.99 quantile gives a value between 1.33 and 5.0, but the text says p99 ≈ 1.33, which corresponds to the 9,900th order statistic (the 'largest non-straggler draw'). The population CDF jumps from 0.99 to 1.0 at 5.0, so the population p99 (smallest x with CDF(x)≥0.99) is 5.0. The 'one extra straggler' sensitivity is correct: with 101 stragglers, the 9,901st value is still a straggler, and the interpolated p99 moves toward 5.0.
root_cause: The explanation prioritizes the conceptual point (sample vs population percentile) over the mechanical point (how linear interpolation on a sorted sample produces the specific value 1.33).
correction: Add a one-sentence mechanical clarification: 'In the sorted sample, the 9,900th value is the largest log-normal draw (~1.33 s) and the 9,901st is the first straggler (5.0 s); the 0.99 quantile falls at rank 9,901, but standard linear interpolation between the 9,900th and 9,901st order statistics at the 0.9999 position yields a value near the 9,900th draw.' Alternatively, add a 3-row mini-table: rank 9,900 → 1.33 s; rank 9,901 → 5.0 s; population p99 → 5.0 s (CDF jump). This makes the knife-edge concrete without adding a full paragraph.
acceptance_test: A reader can explain to a colleague why the sample p99 is 1.33 s but the population p99 is 5.0 s, using the order-statistic mechanism, not just the 'knife-edge' label.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a), 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'

observed: 'Overkill' is informal register for a technical architecture handbook. The surrounding sentence provides the quantitative reasoning (unquantified quality gain must clear a ~3× FLOP bar), so the word is doing no additional work beyond the reasoning.
evidence: The sentence continues: 'its quality gain over all-mpnet-base-v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics), and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64-token embedding in the table above, the same ratio as their parameter counts) — validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it.' The quantitative argument is complete without 'overkill.'
root_cause: Colloquial phrasing slipped into a formal recommendation paragraph.
correction: Replace 'is overkill for this scale' with 'is not justified at this scale' or 'exceeds what this workload's compute budget warrants without a quantified quality gain.'
acceptance_test: The sentence reads at the same register as the surrounding technical prose.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(c), the Q* formula scope note
quoted_clause: (Scope: this Q* amortizes only the one-time training + carry cost against the quality uplift; it omits the recurring per-query prefill/retrieval saving that fine-tuning's shorter context (§5.3(c)) would confer, so it is a lower bound on the fine-tuning case and overstates the break-even volume.)
observed: The scope limitation is important (the formula is not the full economic comparison) but is buried in a long parenthetical at the end of a dense paragraph. A reader who skims the paragraph may miss it and treat Q* as the complete break-even criterion.
evidence: The parenthetical is 45 words and contains a cross-reference (§5.3(c)) and a directional claim ('lower bound on the fine-tuning case and overstates the break-even volume'). The main text before it says 'The economic comparison should be framed parametrically, not with a single number, because the break-even depends on the quality uplift (domain-specific) and the query volume (workload-specific).' The scope note adds a further limitation not captured by that sentence.
root_cause: The scope note was added as a post-hoc clarification rather than integrated into the main argument structure.
correction: Promote the scope note to a standalone sentence immediately after the formula, before the 'Below Q*' explanation: 'Note: this formula captures only the one-time training and carry cost amortized against the quality uplift. The Q* above is therefore a conservative (higher) estimate of the queries needed to justify fine-tuning.'
acceptance_test: A reader who stops after the formula and the 'Below Q*' sentence still understands that the formula is incomplete and in which direction it is incomplete.

page_hint: Ch 8, §6, 'From video dimensions to repeated attention work' — the Wan2.2 TI2V-5B worked example
quoted_clause: A worked example makes the new work unit concrete. We use Wan2.2 TI2V-5B in its text-to-video path, not the A14B expert model. Its configuration specifies a dense transformer with hidden width 3,072, 30 layers, and 24 attention heads. The VAE has 48 latent channels and temporal/spatial strides of 4, 16, and 16. The denoiser patches the latent video by (1,2,2). The release's '720P' example is precisely 1,280 × 704 pixels, 121 frames, at 24 frames/s. The dimensions, rather than the marketing resolution label, determine the budget.
observed: The Wan2.2 example is ~800 words of dense arithmetic spanning geometry (latent dimensions, patching), FLOP counting (attention core, per-layer, per-branch, total trajectory), memory (hidden tensor, score tensor), and sensitivity (frame count, spatial scaling). While every number is correct, the example introduces 15+ new quantities (T_l, H_l, W_l, N, d, C_attention, branch count, timestep count, BF16 hidden size, score tensor size, frame-to-second conversion) in a single continuous block. A reader who loses the thread at any point must re-read the entire section. The example's intellectual job is to show that 'fewer sequential evaluations can mean more total work' (the §1 principle) in a non-AR context, but the density obscures that connection.
evidence: All calculations verified: T_l=31, H_l=44, W_l=80, N=27,280, C_attention=9.145 TFLOP/layer, 274.341 TFLOP/branch, 27.434 PFLOP total, 167,608,320 B hidden, 35,721,523,200 B score, 33.268 GiB, 1.968× token scaling, 3.872× pairwise scaling, 5.0417 s. The example is arithmetically sound but pedagogically dense.
root_cause: The example was written to be comprehensive (covering geometry, FLOPs, memory, and sensitivity) rather than to illustrate one specific principle with minimal supporting detail.
correction: Restructure with explicit sub-steps: (1) 'Geometry: from pixels to tokens' (T_l, H_l, W_l, N — 4 lines); (2) 'Attention FLOPs per evaluation' (C_attention formula, per-layer, per-branch — 4 lines); (3) 'Total trajectory work' (branch count, timesteps, total PFLOP — 3 lines); (4) 'Memory boundary' (hidden tensor, score tensor, FlashAttention note — 4 lines); (5) 'Sensitivity' (frame scaling, spatial scaling, time convention — 4 lines). Add a one-sentence bridge at the start: 'This example applies the §1 principle (fewer sequential evaluations ≠ less total work) to a whole-clip denoiser, where 50 timesteps × 2 CFG branches = 100 evaluations each process all 27,280 tokens simultaneously.' The sensitivity and memory sections could be moved to a 'Further detail' sub-paragraph or a sidebar if the main text's purpose is the FLOP-counting principle.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the example's single main point (100 evaluations × 27,280 tokens = large total work despite few sequential steps) within 30 seconds of starting the section, without needing to follow all 15+ intermediate quantities.

page_hint: Ch 7, Fig 7.7 caption and the 'Technical note — per-rank fit' paragraph
quoted_clause: the 140 GB of weights shard to ~17.5 GB per GPU; the ~64 GB runtime/NCCL reserve is per-host (not per-rank); the ~436 GB KV budget shards to ~54.5 GB per GPU; and under tensor-parallel attention the per-request KV (24.9 GB) also shards across the 8 ranks, so the per-rank KV per request is ~3.1 GB. The 17.5 concurrent figure is therefore the aggregate bound — a rank can be the binding constraint even when the aggregate fits
observed: The per-rank arithmetic is correct (140/8=17.5; 436/8=54.5; 24.9/8=3.11≈3.1) and the caveat is important. However, the paragraph is dense with five distinct per-rank quantities in a single sentence, and the key insight (aggregate fit ≠ per-rank fit) is stated at the end after the reader has already processed all the numbers. The 'Technical note' label suggests it is supplementary, but it contains the most architecturally important caveat in the figure's context.
evidence: 140/8 = 17.5 ✓; 436/8 = 54.5 ✓; 24.9/8 = 3.1125 ≈ 3.1 ✓; 17.5 + 3.1 = 20.6 GB per rank for one request's weights + KV, well within 80 GB per rank. The aggregate 17.5 concurrent is correct; per-rank, 17.5 requests × 3.1 GB = 54.25 GB KV + 17.5 GB weights = 71.75 GB per rank, leaving 8.25 GB for runtime — tight but the text correctly says 'per-rank fit and sharding must be validated separately.'
root_cause: The per-rank breakdown was added as a clarification to the aggregate figure but was written as a single dense sentence rather than a structured list.
correction: Present the per-rank quantities as a short list or 2×3 table: (weights/rank: 17.5 GB; runtime/rank: 8 GB [64/8]; KV/rank per request: 3.1 GB; total per rank at 17.5 concurrent: 17.5 + 8 + 54.25 = 79.75 GB ≈ 80 GB). Then state the insight: 'At 17.5 concurrent requests, per-rank utilization reaches ~99.7% of the 80 GB rank capacity, leaving no room for fragmentation or workspace growth. The aggregate 17.5 is therefore a hard ceiling, not a comfortable operating point.' This makes the caveat concrete and actionable.
acceptance_test: A reader can see the per-rank budget at the 17.5-concurrent point and understand why it is a ceiling rather than a comfortable target, without re-deriving the five quantities from the prose.

page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Goodput vs Raw Throughput' — the 50→70 tok/s example
quoted_clause: suppose we enable larger dynamic batching to raise raw tokens/s from 50 tok/s to 70 tok/s (Chapter 5's low-batch decode basis, ~20 ms/token in that worked example — canonical batch-1 at 25 ms/token is 40 tok/s — a low-batch operating point, not the host's aggregate serving rate; Chapter 15's ~8.5K tok/s is prefill-side and its ~35,000–56,000 tok/s the batched serving rate), but the batch window pushes p95 TTFT from 1.8 s to 2.3 s

The reader is in the middle of a goodput argument (50→70 tok/s, p95 1.8→2.3 s) and is stopped to reconcile four different token-rate figures from three chapters. The information is correct and necessary for scope discipline, but its placement breaks the example's momentum.
evidence: All referenced figures are correct: Ch 5's 50 tok/s (20 ms/token) is [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; canonical batch-1 is 40 tok/s (25 ms/token); Ch 15's ~8.5K tok/s is prefill-side; ~35,000–56,000 tok/s is batched serving. The parenthetical correctly prevents the reader from mistaking 50 tok/s for the host's aggregate rate.

They are not the host's aggregate serving rate (Ch 15: ~35,000–56,000 tok/s under continuous batching) or the prefill-side rate (~8.5K tok/s). page_hint: Ch 5, §2, 'Mental Model' — the input-heavy vs output-heavy paragraph
quoted_clause: If the workload is input-heavy (9.2K average input, 300-token output, ~30× more input than output), the system is first-order memory-capacity-bound (KV residency at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs — a first-order tendency to verify per workload, not a consequence of input-heaviness alone. If the workload were output-heavy, the token/FLOP mix shifts toward decode, which often makes decode bandwidth or latency critical — the actual bottleneck must be measured on the target stack.
observed: The paragraph correctly hedges both claims ('first-order tendency to verify per workload,' 'the actual bottleneck must be measured'). However, the phrase 'memory-capacity-bound' is used without the full three-bound distinction that Ch 8 §1 establishes (compute-bound vs memory-bandwidth-bound vs memory-capacity-constrained). A reader encountering this in Ch 5 (before Ch 8) may conflate 'memory-capacity-bound' with 'memory-bandwidth-bound.' The Ch 8 distinction is the correct one, but Ch 5 uses the term before it is defined.
evidence: Ch 8 §1: 'Three different bounds — keep them apart. Compute-bound means... Memory-bandwidth-bound (what the roofline calls memory-bound) means... Memory-capacity-constrained (often KV-capacity-constrained in long-context inference) means feasible concurrency or context is limited by how much data fits in HBM.' Ch 5's 'memory-capacity-bound' matches the third definition but the reader has not yet seen the distinction.
root_cause: Ch 5 uses a term that is precisely defined in Ch 8, creating a forward-dependency on a distinction the reader has not yet learned.
correction: Either (a) add a brief inline definition: 'first-order memory-capacity-bound (the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit — distinct from memory-bandwidth-bound, where the rate of HBM reads limits per-token speed; Ch 8 §1 formalizes the three-way distinction)'; or (b) rephrase to avoid the term: 'first-order limited by KV-cache HBM capacity (the per-request KV footprint constrains concurrency at the Ch 17 screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs.' Option (b) is simpler and avoids the forward reference.
acceptance_test: A reader who has not yet read Ch 8 can distinguish the 'memory-capacity' constraint (how many requests fit) from a 'memory-bandwidth' constraint (how fast each token is produced) based on Ch 5's text alone.

page_hint: Ch 7, §1, 'Count state by lifetime, not by the model label' — the 256-position canvas example
quoted_clause: As a shape-only example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary needs 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456 bytes, or 256 MiB, for one FP32 logits tensor at batch one. This excludes probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers and the rest of the model. It is not a measured model footprint.
observed: The calculation is correct (256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456 = 256 MiB). However, the example's purpose (illustrating that a diffusion runtime's peak memory is not captured by the AR weights+KV formula) is not made explicit before the number. The reader must infer why a 256 MiB logits tensor is relevant to the 'count state by lifetime' principle. The sentence 'This excludes probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers and the rest of the model' is a list of exclusions that does not help the reader understand what the 256 MiB figure is *for*.
evidence: 256 × 262,144 = 67,108,864; × 4 = 268,435,456 B = 256 MiB. ✓. The point is that a single intermediate tensor (logits for 256 positions) can be 256 MiB, which is non-trivial relative to a 24 GB device's budget, and that this tensor is not part of the AR KV cache formula.
root_cause: The example was written as a shape calculation without a preceding sentence stating the architectural point it illustrates.
correction: Prepend one sentence: 'A diffusion runtime's peak memory includes intermediate tensors (logits, attention scores, sampling buffers) that have no analogue in the AR weights+KV formula. For example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary produces a single FP32 logits tensor of 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 256 MiB at batch one — a non-trivial fraction of a 24 GB device's budget, and a cost the AR formula does not capture. This excludes the remaining model state (probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers, weights).'
acceptance_test: A reader can state in one sentence why the 256 MiB figure matters for the 'count state by lifetime' principle, without re-reading the paragraph.

page_hint: Ch 8, §3, 'Prefill PFLOP for 9.2K input' — the initial 1.29 PFLOP figure
quoted_clause: the prefill FLOP cost is: 2 × N × L = 2 × 70 × 10^9 × 9.2 × 10^3 ≈ 1.29 PFLOP [DERIVED: 2 × N × L where N=70B, L=9,200; the figure is large because the full context is attended to, but it is a one-time cost per request, not a sustained rate]
observed: The 1.29 PFLOP figure is presented as 'the prefill FLOP cost' before the three-case accounting (linear-only, full-square, causal-triangle) is introduced two paragraphs later. The [DERIVED] note says 'the figure is large because the full context is attended to' which is slightly misleading: the 2NL figure is large because it multiplies by L, but the 'full context is attended to' phrase suggests the attention term is included, when it is not. The reader may carry the 1.29 as the 'true' prefill cost until the three-case section corrects it.
evidence: The 2NL = 1.288 PFLOP is the linear-only (case i) figure. The full-square (case ii) is 1.5099 PFLOP (+17.23%). The causal (case iii) is 1.3989 PFLOP (+8.61%). The [DERIVED] note's phrase 'the figure is large because the full context is attended to' conflates the linear scaling with L (which is correct) with the attention mechanism (which is the quadratic term, not included in 2NL).
root_cause: The initial figure was written as a simple 2NL calculation with a brief note, before the three-case section was added. The note's language was not updated to reflect that the attention term is excluded.
correction: Change the [DERIVED] note to: '[DERIVED: 2 × N × L where N=70B, L=9,200; this is the linear (projection) term only — the quadratic attention term adds ~17% at 9.2K (case (ii), below). The figure is a one-time cost per request, not a sustained rate.]' This prevents the reader from treating 1.29 as the complete prefill cost.
acceptance_test: A reader who stops after the 1.29 PFLOP figure and its [DERIVED] note understands that the attention term is not included, without needing to read the three-case section.

page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Detecting the Regime' — the decode bandwidth paragraph
quoted_clause: Within a ~25 ms TPOT budget that demands 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s (batch-1-equivalent) of HBM bandwidth, against an H100's ~3.35 TB/s peak [1P][FACT]. Scope warning: this 5.6-vs-3.35 TB/s comparison is an illustrative single-device roofline argument, not the canonical 8×H100 host's actual deployment verdict.
observed: The scope warning is important and correct, but it is placed *after* the 5.6-vs-3.35 comparison, which a reader may have already internalized as a 'the H100 can't do decode' verdict before reading the warning. The two scope notes (single-device vs 8×H100; aggregate vs per-rank) are then stated in a dense paragraph. The key insight (decode is bandwidth-bound because of low arithmetic intensity, not because 5.6 > 3.35) is buried at the end of the paragraph.
evidence: The 5.6 TB/s is the aggregate model-wide weight-read rate for a hypothetical single-device implementation. Under TP=8, each GPU reads 140/8 = 17.5 GB per token, requiring 17.5/0.025 = 0.7 TB/s against its 3.35 TB/s — well within capacity. The bandwidth-bound classification follows from the 1.0 FLOP/byte intensity (far below the 295 ridge), not from the 5.6 > 3.35 comparison. The text states all this correctly but in an order that risks the reader anchoring on the 5.6-vs-3.35 number first.
root_cause: The paragraph was structured as 'calculation → comparison → scope warning → deeper reason,' but the pedagogically effective order is 'deeper reason (intensity) → calculation (for illustration) → scope (why the calculation is not the verdict).'
correction: Restructure: (1) State the intensity argument first: 'Decode at batch 1 has an arithmetic intensity of ~1.0 FLOP/byte (140 GFLOP / 140 GB), far below the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge — this is why decode is bandwidth-bound, regardless of how many GPUs are used.' (2) Then give the single-device illustration: 'As a concrete single-device illustration: 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s exceeds one H100's 3.35 TB/s peak. Under TP=8, each GPU reads only 17.5 GB (0.7 TB/s), so the per-GPU bandwidth is not the binding constraint — the low intensity is.' (3) Then the scope note: 'This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch, decode intensity rises and can approach the ridge.'
acceptance_test: A reader who reads only the first two sentences of the restructured paragraph can state why decode is bandwidth-bound (low intensity) and why the 5.6-vs-3.35 comparison is illustrative rather than verdictal.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b), 'Economics unit note (reconciliation with Ch. 4 and Ch. 15)'
quoted_clause: Both chapters use the same on-demand price basis: ~$2.50/hr per H100 → ~$20/hr per 8×H100 host. Two things must be kept straight. First, units: both chapters express tokens per dollar — this chapter computes it as token-rate × 3600 s ÷ hourly cost (50 × 3600 ÷ 20 = 9,000 tokens per dollar), which is algebraically identical to token-rate ÷ per-second cost (50 ÷ (20/3600) = 9,000); no 3600 factor separates the two formulas.
observed: The reconciliation note is correct and addresses a real potential confusion (the 3600 factor). However, it is 120 words long and appears in the middle of the worked example's economics section, interrupting the flow from the 9,000 tokens/$ calculation to the prefill+decode combined calculation. The note's purpose is to prevent a specific misreading (that Ch 4 and Ch 15 use a different formula), but its length and placement make it feel like a digression rather than a clarification.
